reason: While the text describes Yahweh selling Israel to their enemies (Jabin) as punishment for doing evil, this represents divine judgment for transgression, not antagonism toward the people themselves. The narrative demonstrates a redemptive pattern: (1) Israel sins and is punished through oppression; (2) Israel cries out to Yahweh; (3) Yahweh responds through the prophetess Deborah with active military aid; (4) Yahweh personally defeats Sisera and his forces ('Yahweh confounded Sisera...before Barak'); (5) the hand of Israel grows stronger until they destroy their oppressor. Critically, Yahweh explicitly goes out before them in battle (יְהוָה יָצָא לְפָנֶיךָ), orchestrates the victory, and subdues the Canaanite king. This shows protective, salvific action toward Israel, not antagonism. The punishment is corrective—a response to evil—followed by deliverance once Israel repents.
